JURISDICTION  CRIMINAL APPEAL No.5147/2025  [Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.13757/2024]
GAJANAN SITARAM CHAUDHARI APPELLANT  VERSUS  STATE OF MAHARASTHRA & ORS. RESPONDENTS  ORDER 1.
Leave granted.

2. Appellant is a driver employed by the Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation1,
respondent no.2.

He was tried by the court of the Judicial Magistrate First Class, at Khed-Rajgurunagar, District Pune for alleged commission of offence punishable under Sections 279,
338 & 304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
3.

entities.text: Judicial Magistrate First Class, at Khed-Rajgurunagar, District Pune
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: According to the prosecution, on 4th May, 2012 around 8:30 pm, Hanumant Ankush Nikam (respondent no.3) and his wife, Rani Hanumant Nikam2, were returning home on a motorcycle.
The victim was the pillion rider.

At a particular junction (chowk) on the Pune-Nashik highway, when the respondent no.3 had stopped the motorcycle in response to flashing of 1 Corporation 2 victim the red light, a bus of the Corporation driven recklessly and negligently by the appellant came from behind and dashed the motorcycle.
The victim fell in front of the bus and the left-side wheel of the bus dashed her head, as a result of which she suffered serious head injury.
She was immediately shifted to a local hospital where ultimately succumbed to the injury.
Appellant was charged with Gajanan Sitaram Chaudhari vs State Of Maharasthra on 2 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/116077563/

sentences.text: 1 rash and negligent driving resulting in the accidental death of the victim.
4. The Judicial Magistrate found the appellant guilty and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for two years together with a fine of Rs.1,500/-, vide judgment and order dated 7th February, 2014.

5. Appellant carried the conviction and sentence in appeal before the Additional Sessions Judge,
Khed-Rajgurunagar, District Pune.

Additional Sessions Judge,
Khed-Rajgurunagar, District Pune
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
Vide judgment and order dated 05th November, 2019, the Additional Sessions Judge upheld the verdict of the Judicial Magistrate.
6.
Aggrieved thereby, the appellant approached the High Court of Judicature at Bombay by filing a revisional application3.

entities.text: High Court of Judicature at Bombay
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
7. Upon hearing the parties, a learned Judge of the High Court recorded in paragraphs 9 and 13 of his judgment dated 11th December, 2023 as follows:
9.
After examining the record of the case, it is revealed that Hanumant Nikam (PW 1) was the husband of the deceased Rani.
They were returning to their village on a motorcycle after attending a marriage at Bhosari.
Hanumant (PW 1) was driving the motorcycle while his wife Rani was riding the pillion.
They stopped at Chakan Talegaon Square due to a red light signal.

The offending bus bearing registration No.MH-12-CH-7606 came from behind and knocked down to their motorcycle,
causing Rani/the deceased to fall off the motorcycle and sustain a head injury from the wheel of the bus.

13. The incident occurred on a road with heavy traffic 3 Criminal Revision Application No.83/2020 where several vehicles, including the informant's motorcycle had come to a stop due to a red light signal.

Despite the circumstances,
the accused drove his vehicle recklessly and negligently, causing the death of the wife of the informant.
It is evident that a prudent person would not drive a bus in such a manner as to collide with a motorcycle that had stopped due to red light signal.
This act is certainly negligent and reckless, and demonstrates a lack of due care and attention.
Based on the aforesaid findings, the High Court dismissed the revision.
8. This appeal is directed against the revisional judgment and order dated 11th December, 2023 of the High Court.

9. According to Mr. Cheema, learned counsel appearing for the appellant, it is not disputed that the appellant was driving the Corporation bus on the fateful evening and that later, he was taken by the police.

However, he has raised the following points to seek reversal of the conviction and sentence:
A. No independent witness was examined, though the highway was crowded with vehicles and people.

Gajanan Sitaram Chaudhari vs State Of Maharasthra on 2 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/116077563/
2 B.

sentences.text: There is material contradiction in the statements of the respondent no.3 before the police and in the court.

Before the police, while it was stated by the respondent no.3 that the victim fell and the wheel on the cleaner side of the bus struck her head, in examination- in-chief, he deposed that the bus dashed from behind and the head of the victim got crushed under the wheel.
Distinction was sought to be drawn between the head striking a hard object like a wheel and the head being crushed under the weight of the wheel.
C. There is no evidence that the head of the victim was crushed under the left wheel of the bus.
On the contrary, the medical evidence is that injury could have occurred even upon a fall on a hard surface when a vehicle is in high speed.
D. When a motorcycle is dashed from behind by a bus being driven rashly and negligently, it is logical that both the riders would fall and sustain some injury.
However, there is no evidence of the respondent no.3 having suffered any injury.
E. There is an unexplained delay of 5 (five) days in lodging of the complaint by the respondent no.3.
F. Spot panchanama was not prepared on the day of the accident but on the following day and that at a distance from the place of occurrence.

10. From the trend of cross-examination as well as in course of explaining circumstances under Section 313, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the defence case appears to be that the bus driven by the appellant had stopped because of the red signal at the junction and that it was stationary allowing passengers to de-board; however, the respondent no.3 while riding the motorcycle lost control resulting in a fall of the victim; and, in the process, she might have accidentally struck the surface of the road or the stationary bus causing head injury, which resulted in her death.

11. On perusal of the evidence on record, we find the respondent no.3 (as PW-1) having deposed on 30th November, 2013 that because of the bus dashing his stationary motorcycle from behind, the victim fell from her seat and her head was crushed by the wheel of the bus.
Respondent no.3 did not state whether the victim was wearing a helmet, a mandatory requirement in terms of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 4, which could have saved her life.
In any event, it was not the defence case that the victims life would have been saved if she wore a helmet.
However, it is rather strange that the impact of the bus dashing the motorcycle from behind resulted in the victim falling, but the respondent no.3 neither fell from his seat nor suffered any injury.

Without anything more, if the evidence of the respondent no.3 is to be believed, it probabilises that the appellant drove the bus rashly and negligently, dashed the motorcycle whereupon the victim fell down, suffered head injury because the left wheel crushed her head and she ultimately died.

3 12.

sentences.text: There are, however, certain doubtful circumstances which need to be noted at this stage.
Nothing was specifically stated by the respondent no.3 with regard to the nature of damage that was caused to the motorcycle by reason of its impact with the bus.

Despite the respondent no.3 deposing that there were sufficient lights on the highway and heavy traffic as well as traffic police on the road,
neither any policeman or passer-by on the highway nor any of the passengers of the bus was examined.
Apart from the respondent no.3, there was thus no independent witness who testified with regard to the accident that took away the life of the victim.
There is also no evidence of whether it was the front left wheel or the rear left wheel that crushed/struck the victims head.
13. Was it safe to record a conviction based on the uncorroborated testimony of the respondent no.3?

Were the appellate and revisional courts justified in placing complete reliance on the testimony of the respondent no.3 without considering the other evidence on record which create 4 MV Act substantial doubt?
We would now endeavour to seek answers to this questions.
14. Mr. Cheemas submission relying on the medical evidence has substance.
The post-mortem report prepared by the doctor at the Rural Hospital (PW-4) has been perused.
He found a fractured skull.
Had the head of the victim been crushed under the weight of the wheel of a heavy vehicle like a Corporation bus, what would normally have remained is a mangled head.

That the head was not in mangled state is a relevant circumstance for us to hold that none of the wheels on the left side alignment of the bus crushed the victims head; although, it could be so, that impact with the bus or its wheel was such that the victim died of shock of the nature referred to by PW-4.
To this extent, the version of the respondent no.3 does not inspire confidence.

15. Besides, if the High Court is right (as held in paragraph 13 extracted supra) that the bus was being driven rashly and negligently and had dashed the motorcycle, when it had stopped at the red signal, which is a negligent and reckless act on the part of the appellant, it is natural and would indeed be a relevant circumstance that the motorcycle must have suffered some damage.
Respondent no.3 vaguely said in his cross-examination that the motorcycle was damaged.
16. We have looked into the evidence of PW-2, Shivaji Bhagwan Savant, being one of the seizure witnesses.
A damaged motorcycle would have immediately caught the attention of none other than the witness to the seizure thereof.
In course of cross examination, PW-2 could not throw any light about the motorcycle having suffered any damage because of the impact.
There is no other evidence on record to suggest that the motorcycle did suffer any damage and, thus, it creates a cloud of suspicion as to the nature and extent of the impact.

17. These circumstances coupled with the fact that the respondent no.3 lodged the written complaint on 9th May, 2012 without any plausible explanation for the delay (the accident occurred on 4 th May, 2012) made us embark on a more intrusive scrutiny of the materials on record.

18. We had the occasion to look into the award passed by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal,
Pune5 dated 22nd July, 2016 on an application6 under Section 166 of the MV Act preferred by the respondent no.3 seeking compensation owing to the accidental death of the victim in the accident which occurred on 4th May, 2012.

By such award, the tribunal awarded Rs.12,45,000/- as just Gajanan Sitaram Chaudhari vs State Of Maharasthra on 2 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/116077563/
4 compensation to the respondent no.3.
19.

sentences.text:
Issue no.1, which was framed by the tribunal, and its discussion of the evidence led by the respondent no.3 as claimant, being AW1, read thus:
6. *
* * * Sr.No.1

Whether the applicants have proved that Sau. Rani Hanumant Nikam died in the vehicular accident, caused on 04/05/2012 at about 08-30 p.m. by rash and negligent driving of MSRTC Bus No.MH/12/CH/7606?
9.
As to Issue no.1:- AW-1 Hanumant Nikam is an eye witness to the accident.
He was riding the motorcycle 5 tribunal
Deceased Rani was pillion rider on the motorcycle.
They were proceeding on motorcycle from Pune side to Khed side.

Therefore,
evidence of AW-1 Hanumant is an important to assess the negligent and rash driving of the offending Bus.
He deposed that on said fateful day, he reached to Talegaon chowk.
He specifically deposed that the offending Bus came behind the motorcycle.
The offending Bus was in high speed.
Its driver was driving the same in rashly and negligently and gave dash to the motorcycle.
He deposed that as a result, deceased Rani fell down on the road, and came under left rear wheel of the offending Bus and then succumbed to death.
He was cross-examined at length.
His evidence has not been shaken.
He was suggested that, he was negligent and rash, but he boldly and unambiguously denied said suggestion.
It is also suggested to him that he was overtaking the offending Bus from conductor side and dashed to the offending bus.
He has also denied said suggestion boldly.

It is needless to say that if suggestion is denied boldly,
same cannot take the place of evidence.
In the absence of any material admission from the mouth of AW-1, I have no hesitation to discard his evidence.
(emphasis ours)
21. A bare perusal of the contents of paragraph 9 of the award would reveal a somewhat different version of how the accident occurred.

Although it is evident that the respondent no.3 had denied the suggestions put to him of the accident having occurred while he was overtaking the bus from the left side and he himself dashed the bus, what stands out is that the bus, according to him, was being operated in high speed and its driver was rash and negligent; and while the bus dashed the motorcycle, the victim fell down on the road and came under the left rear wheel of the bus resulting in her death.
22. It is noteworthy that the appellant was not a party to the proceedings before the tribunal and had no opportunity to cross-examine the respondent no.3.

Be that as it may, it is clear from the evidence led before the tribunal that the respondent no.3 said something more in order to obtain an Gajanan Sitaram Chaudhari vs State Of Maharasthra on 2 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/116077563/
5 award from the tribunal to compensate for the loss of life of the victim.
23.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Juxtaposing the evidence that the respondent no.3 led before the Judicial Magistrate with the evidence led before the tribunal, the conclusion is irresistible that the versions are at variance.

The version of the respondent no.3 given before the tribunal that the victim came under the left rear wheel of the bus having been accepted, which led to the award of just compensation being assessed in a sum of Rs.12,45,000/- payable by the Corporation, we feel hesitant to accept his uncorroborated version in course of the trial.
24.
Varying outcomes, from conflicting versions of the same accident presented in different fora, are not acceptable.
25. We may place on record that despite the respondent no.3 being put on notice, he has refrained from participating in the proceedings before us.

26. Taking an overall view of the matter, we are of the considered opinion that there is a reasonable doubt as to how the accident occurred and whether at all the appellant was guilty of rash and negligent driving of the bus resulting in the death of the victim.
The evidence on record does suggest that the respondent no.3 could have himself been on the wrong side of the law while driving the motorcycle and not the appellant.

In our view, the Judicial Magistrate, the Additional Sessions Judge as well as the High Court fell in error in returning the finding that it is because of rash and negligent driving of the bus by the appellant that resulted in the victims death instead of extending the benefit of doubt to the appellant.
27. We, therefore, set aside the conviction and sentence imposed on the appellant.
He is set free and discharged of his bail bond.
28. The appeal, thus, stands allowed.
